title: Ethnic tension builds in Montreal; Anger, rioting after teen shot by police
article: The sister of an 18-year-old man shot and killed by police Saturday night is calling for calm after Sunday night's violent riots in Montreal North.
"We never wanted to see something like that," said Patricia Villanueva.
"What's rioting going to change? It's not going to bring my brother back."
Her brother, Fredy Villanueva, was killed in a confrontation between two police officers and a group of young men he was hanging out with Saturday.
Police said the officers felt threatened, but witnesses at the scene told a different story -- one in which Fredy was shot after little provocation.

On Sunday, residents of Montreal North marched through the streets, peacefully protesting the shooting. But around 11 p.m., the protest turned violent, with knots of people roaming the streets and setting fire to cars, propane tanks and garbage bins.
The Montreal riot police were called out and some 500 officers arrived on the scene to try to re-establish law and order.
At the Villanueva house, Fredy's brother and sisters struggled to make sense of the death.
His sister, Julissa, said the violent turn of last night's march left a bitter taste in her mouth.
"We're devastated. Our family is feeling absolutely broken, and things like this are the last things we want to see," she said.

Both Patricia and Julissa said they were relieved to see their brother, Dany, who was with Fredy when he was shot on Saturday. Dany was getting arrested, wrestled to the ground, when Fredy and a group of friends walked towards police. The two officers then started firing, hitting Fredy and two of his friends.

Back at home after a short stint in jail, Dany confirmed witness accounts of the event. He said there was no way police could have felt threatened enough to fire at his brother, because no one at the scene had gotten violent.
"When the policeman had me on the ground, I was face up, I was looking right at him and I didn't see anyone touch him," he said.
Dany was charged with assault for having struggled against police when they tried to arrest him. He says he has no idea why police wanted to take him in to begin with.
"They didn't tell me anything, and they only charged me with assault."
In the wake of the riots, the Montreal police force's track record on race relations came into sharp focus on Monday.
The force says the problems are mostly gang-related, but community leaders say the problems go deeper than that.

"The relationship between young men and the police in these (hot) areas is very difficult," said Maria Mourani, a sociologist and Bloc Quebecois politician who wrote a book about street-gang life in Montreal.
"The police are on edge because, when they get out of their cars, they don't know what is going to happen. The young people are on edge because they feel they are being harassed."
Much of the tension stems from what young people say is racial profiling by police officers who are trying to crack down on street-gang activity.
But in doing that, community leaders say police are harassing too many black and Latino youths with no criminal records and who have no ties to street gangs.
Montreal North is a community of about 84,000 people, dotted with pockets of poverty and rife with street gangs.
During the riot, a female police officer was shot in the thigh and rioters torched cars, looted businesses, and set fire to a fire hall.

Montreal police Chief Yvan Delorme, who appealed for area residents to remain calm on Monday, said the force is working to halt racial profiling and give sensitivity training to all its police officers.
"We're ahead of any police department that we know of. We have to continue to work on that," he said.
Environment Minister Line Beauchamp, whose riding encompasses Montreal North, was the first member of the government to comment on the riot.
"What happened here is an unfortunate event, but will not set us back," said Beauchamp, who has been living in Montreal North for 10 years.
Beauchamp added the Quebec provincial police has launched an inquiry into the weekend events and promised their findings will be made public.
